qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Phase eight. Cryptography and blockchain. This is how secrets and trust work online.
Alice sends Bob SECRET along an open wire, and Eve can read it.
Anything on the open wire, Eve can read.
A shift cipher with key five moves each letter five along, so S becomes X. Eve cannot read that.
The key is 5: each letter moves 5 along, so S becomes X.
But Bob needs the key too, and Eve would copy it from the wire.
But how does Bob get the key without Eve seeing it?
Alice and Bob each start with the same public paint.
Both start with the same public paint.
Each mixes in a secret paint of their own.
Each adds a secret paint of their own.
They swap the mixtures in public, so Eve sees both.
They swap the mixtures. Eve can see those.
Each adds their secret to the mixture they got, and the pots match.
Each adds their own secret again: the very same colour.
That shared colour becomes their key.
That colour is their shared key.
Eve sees both mixtures, but she cannot unmix paint.
Eve cannot unmix paint to find a secret.
Twenty-three and five are public. Alice's secret is six, and Bob's is fifteen.
Like the paint: p and g are public, a and b secret.
Alice works out five to the power six, keeping only the remainder after dividing by twenty-three.
mod 23 keeps only the remainder after dividing by 23.
Alice gets eight, Bob gets nineteen, and they swap them in public.
They swap A = 8 and B = 19 in public.
Each raises what they got to their own secret.
Each raises what they received to their own secret.
Both get two. That shared key was never sent.
Both get 2: a shared key that was never sent.
Eve must try powers of five until one gives eight.
Eve must try every power of 5 until she hits 8: that finds a.
With a real prime of six hundred and seventeen digits, that search is hopeless.
With a 617-digit prime that search is hopeless.
Bob picks two secret prime numbers, five and eleven.
Pick two secret primes: 5 and 11.
He multiplies them to get fifty-five, which is public.
Multiply them: n = 55 is public.
Next he takes one off each prime, multiplies, and keeps forty secret.
Next z = (5 − 1) × (11 − 1) = 40, kept secret.
He picks three, because three and forty share no factor except one.
Pick e = 3: only 1 divides both 3 and 40.
Twenty-seven pairs with it, because three times twenty-seven is two forties plus one.
The public key is fifty-five and three. The private key, twenty-seven, stays secret.
Publish (55, 3). Keep 27 secret.
Bob shares his public key, fifty-five and three, along the open wire.
Bob shares his public key, (55, 3).
Alice locks the number seven with it, and gets thirteen.
Alice locks 7 with it and gets 13.
Bob unlocks thirteen with his private key, and gets seven back.
Bob unlocks 13 with his private key: back to 7.
Eve can factor such a tiny number in four tries.
Eve factors the tiny n in four tries: 5 × 11.
Then she gets forty and twenty-seven, and has the key.
Then z = 40 and d = 27: she has the key.
A real number has over six hundred digits, and nobody can factor it.
A real n has 617+ digits: nobody can factor that.
Next comes trust, and whether data was changed.
New question: was this data changed?
A hash turns data, like the word cat, into a short fingerprint.
A hash turns data into a short fingerprint.
Hash the same word again, and the fingerprint is exactly the same.
The same data always gives the same fingerprint.
Change one letter, to make cot, and every digit changes.
Change one letter, the whole fingerprint changes.
And there is no way back from the fingerprint to the data.
And you cannot work backwards from it.
In a chain, each block stores the hash of the block before it.
Each block stores the hash of the block before it.
Now someone edits the first block, and its hash changes.
Edit one block and its hash changes.
The next block still holds the old hash, so the link breaks.
The next block holds the old hash: the link breaks.
Eve recomputes each later hash, block by block, to repair the links.
Eve recomputes each later hash to repair the links.
It looks valid again. Hashes can spot edits, but cannot prevent them.
It looks valid again, but hashes only spot edits.
A miner tries numbers, called nonces, until the hash starts with zero.
Try numbers (nonces) until the hash starts with 0.
Every try gives a new, unpredictable hash, so it is all guesswork.
Every try gives a new, unpredictable hash.
The winner is found after fifteen hashes.
Found it after 15 hashes.
Checking it takes just one hash.
Checking takes just 1 hash.
On average, one hash in sixteen starts with a zero.
One hash in 16 starts with 0.
Two zeros come one time in two hundred and fifty-six, so sixteen times more work.
Two zeros: 1 in 256, so 16 times more work.
Now each block is sealed by its own proof of work.
Each block is sealed by its own proof of work.
Edit block one, and its seal and link break.
Edit block 1: its seal and the link both break.
To forge it, Eve must mine block one again.
Forging it means mining block 1 again.
Then every later block must be mined again too.
Then every later block must be mined again too.
Here that costs fifty tries. Real blocks need trillions, so rewriting history means redoing all that work.
Rewriting history means redoing all that work.
A shared secret can be made without ever being sent.
Anyone can lock with the public key, but only Bob can open.
In a blockchain, hashes link the blocks, and edits cost real work.
